title: The Power of Small Wins
text:
Teresa Amabile of Harvard Business School and her husband and research partner Steven Kramer wanted to know what actually happens inside people's heads during an ordinary working day. They recruited 238 professionals working on creative projects in 26 teams across seven companies, and asked each of them to fill out a short diary survey by email every working day of their project, often for months.

The participants rated their mood, motivation and perceptions of their work, and described one event that stood out that day. In total the researchers collected nearly 12,000 diary entries.

When Amabile and Kramer compared the best and worst days, one factor stood out above all others. On days when people made progress in meaningful work, even a small step forward, their mood and motivation were most likely to be high. On the worst days, the most common event was a setback. Progress also fed creativity and productivity, so that good inner days and good work went together. Yet when the researchers surveyed hundreds of managers, very few ranked supporting progress as the top motivator.
lesson: The best thing a leader can do for morale is to clear the way for steady progress on meaningful work, and to remove the obstacles that cause setbacks.
source: Amabile, T., and Kramer, S. (2011). The Progress Principle: Using Small Wins to Ignite Joy, Engagement, and Creativity at Work. Harvard Business Review Press.
